claim: We reliably judge locations of static objects when we walk despite the retinal images of these objects moving with every step we take.
source: We reliably judge locations of static objects when we walk despite the retinal images of these objects moving with every step we take.
evidence: This is a general statement about human perceptual ability that draws from established understanding in vision science.

claim: The brain solves the optical illusion of moving retinal images during walking by adopting an allocentric spatial reference frame.
source: Here, we showed our brains solve this optical illusion by adopting an allocentric spatial reference frame.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The intrinsic bias acts as a spatial reference frame for perceiving location of a dimly lit target in the dark.
source: we found the intrinsic bias , which acts as a spatial reference frame for perceiving location of a dimly lit target in the dark, remained grounded at the home base rather than traveled along with the observer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental findings presented in the manuscript, particularly in Experiment 1.

claim: The intrinsic bias remained grounded at the home base rather than traveled along with the observer.
source: we found the intrinsic bias , which acts as a spatial reference frame for perceiving location of a dimly lit target in the dark, remained grounded at the home base rather than traveled along with the observer.
evidence: This is a key experimental finding supported by data from multiple experiments in the manuscript.

claim: The path-integration mechanism responsible for allocentric coding can utilize both active and passive (vestibular) translational motion signals.
source: The path-integration mechanism responsible for this can utilize both active and passive (vestibular) translational motion signals, but only along the horizontal direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 comparing walking and vestibular conditions.

claim: The path-integration mechanism operates only along the horizontal direction.
source: The path-integration mechanism responsible for this can utilize both active and passive (vestibular) translational motion signals, but only along the horizontal direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 5 (stepladder condition).

claim: The asymmetric path-integration finding in human visual space perception is reminiscent of the asymmetric spatial memory finding in desert ants.
source: This asymmetric path-integration finding in human visual space perception is reminiscent of the asymmetric spatial memory finding in desert ants, pointing to nature's wondrous and logically simple design for terrestrial creatures.
evidence: This is a comparative statement drawing on cited research about desert ants.

claim: The visual system employs the prevalent ground surface as a reference frame for coding spatial locations.
source: Notably, within this phenomenological visual space, our visual system employs the prevalent ground surface, where creatures and objects frequently interact, as a reference frame for coding spatial locations (Gibson, 1950; Sedgwick, 1986; Sinai et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The ground-based spatial coding scheme accurately localizes objects when the horizontal ground surface is continuous and carries rich depth cues.
source: Empirical findings have revealed the ground-based spatial coding scheme accurately localizes objects when the horizontal ground surface is continuous and carries rich depth cues (Thomson, 1983; Rieser et al., 1990; Loomis et al., 1992; Loomis et al., 1996; Sinai et al., 1998; Meng and Sedgwick, 2001; Wu et al., 2004; He et al., 2004; Bian et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Object localization becomes inaccurate when the ground surface is disrupted by a gap or an occluding box.
source: Attesting to the significant role of the ground surface, it has been found that object localization becomes inaccurate when the ground surface is disrupted by a gap or an occluding box (Sinai et al., 1998; He et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Object localization is inaccurate in the dark when the ground is not visible.
source: Similarly, object localization is inaccurate in the dark when the ground is not visible (Ooi et al., 2001; Ooi et al., 2006; Philbeck and Loomis, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The visual system defaults to using an implicit semi-elliptical curved surface representation (intrinsic bias) to localize objects in total darkness.
source: In fact, research conducted in total darkness to prevent the visual system from obtaining depth information from the ground reveals the visual system defaults to using an implicit semi-elliptical curved surface representation that we refer to as the intrinsic bias to localize objects (Ooi et al., 2001; Ooi et al., 2006; Gogel and Tietz, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The intrinsic bias integrates with visible depth cues such as texture gradients on the ground to form a new ground surface representation.
source: This suggests the intrinsic bias, acting as the prototype spatial reference of the ground surface when visual cues are not visible, integrates with the visible depth cues such as texture gradients on the ground to form a new ground surface representation (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The ground surface representation depends on the weighted contributions of the depth information on the ground and the intrinsic bias.
source: In this way, the ground surface representation depends on the weighted contributions of the depth information on the ground and the intrinsic bias.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integration mechanism described in the text and supported by cited research.

claim: During translational movements such as walking, the brain anchors the intrinsic bias at one location on the ground surface using a path-integration mechanism.
source: We proposed that during translational movements, such as walking, the brain anchors the intrinsic bias at one location on the ground surface using a path-integration mechanism (Mittelstaedt and Mittelstaedt, 1980; Wehner and Srinivasan, 1981; Rieser, 1989; Etienne et al., 1996; McNaughton et al., 1996; Loomis et al., 1999; Mittelstaedt and Mittelstaedt, 2001; Loomis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, supported by citations to previous research on path integration and by experimental data.

claim: The path-integration mechanism generates an estimate of the observer's current position relative to their original location (home base) by integrating each step of traveled length and direction.
source: The path-integration mechanism generates an estimate of the observer's current position relative to their original location (home base) by integrating each step of traveled length and direction (vector).
evidence: This is a description of the path-integration mechanism based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: When the observer walks forward in the dark, the path-integration mechanism estimates the walked length by integrating each step length based on inputs from the vestibular and/or proprioception systems.
source: For example, when the observer walks forward in the dark, the path-integration mechanism estimates the walked length by integrating each step length based on inputs from the vestibular and/or proprioception systems.
evidence: This is a description of how path integration works, based on established knowledge and tested in the experiments.

claim: The intrinsic bias shifts behind the body over a distance equaling the estimated walked distance when the observer walks forward.
source: The intrinsic bias accordingly shifts behind the body over a distance equaling the estimated walked distance; effectively placing the intrinsic bias at the home base should the estimated walked distance be accurate.
evidence: This is a prediction of the allocentric hypothesis that is tested and supported by experimental data.

claim: The visual system constructs the ground surface representation from the allocentric intrinsic bias that is fixed to the ground surface at the home base.
source: This leads the visual system to construct the ground surface representation from the (allocentric) intrinsic bias that is fixed to the ground surface at the home base.
evidence: This is a key claim of the allocentric hypothesis supported by experimental data.

claim: The ground-based reference frame can use an allocentric, world-centered, coordinate system to code locations in visual space.
source: Accordingly, the ground-based reference frame can use an allocentric, that is, world-centered, coordinate system to code locations in visual space.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by the experimental findings.

claim: With the 12-s waiting period, judged locations in the walking condition were significantly nearer than in the baseline-stationary condition (p < 0.0001).
source: With the 12 s waiting period, judged locations in the walking condition (filled green triangles) were significantly nearer than the baseline-stationary (filled red circles) condition (p < 0.0001; please refer to the Statistical Analysis of Data at the end of Results section for details of all statistical analyses).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis, also shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The two sets of data points from the 12-s waiting period conditions are fitted by the same shaped intrinsic bias curve with about 1.35 m horizontal separation.
source: The two sets of data points are fitted by the same shaped intrinsic bias curve with about 1.35 m horizontal separation, which is close to the initially walked distance from the home base (1.5 m; in the walking condition).
evidence: This is an analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The horizontal separation of the fitted curves (1.35 m) is close to the initially walked distance from the home base (1.5 m).
source: The two sets of data points are fitted by the same shaped intrinsic bias curve with about 1.35 m horizontal separation, which is close to the initially walked distance from the home base (1.5 m; in the walking condition).
evidence: This is a comparison of the fitted parameter to the experimental condition, supporting the allocentric hypothesis.

claim: With the 60-s waiting period, judged locations in the walking condition had a smaller, though statistically significant, separation from the baseline-stationary condition (p < 0.01).
source: With the 60-s waiting period, judged locations (open triangles) in the walking condition had a smaller, though statistically significant, separation from the baseline-stationary condition (open circles) (p < 0.01).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis, also shown in Figure 3c.

claim: If the waiting period is sufficiently long, the visual memory of the home base decays over time.
source: This suggests if the waiting period was sufficiently long, suggesting the visual memory of the home base decays over time (Thomson, 1983; Loomis et al., 2013), the visual system automatically resets the intrinsic bias to the observer's (new/current) location, that is, making it the updated home base.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 60-s waiting period results, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The visual system automatically resets the intrinsic bias to the observer's new location when visual memory of the home base decays.
source: This suggests if the waiting period was sufficiently long, suggesting the visual memory of the home base decays over time (Thomson, 1983; Loomis et al., 2013), the visual system automatically resets the intrinsic bias to the observer's (new/current) location, that is, making it the updated home base.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results from the 60-s waiting period condition.

claim: The slopes of the regression lines for judged angular declination versus physical angular declination are close to unity.
source: The slopes of the regression lines obtained with the least squared methods are close unity, suggesting perceived angular declinations of the targets were largely accurate.
evidence: This is an analysis of the data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Perceived angular declinations of the targets were largely accurate.
source: The slopes of the regression lines obtained with the least squared methods are close unity, suggesting perceived angular declinations of the targets were largely accurate.
evidence: This is an inference from the regression analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The path-integration mechanism tracks the observer's location with respect to the external world during locomotion.
source: The results above demonstrate the action of the path-integration mechanism. It tracks the observer's location with respect to the external world during locomotion and plays a critical role in maintaining an allocentric reference frame.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results of Experiment 1.

claim: The path-integration mechanism plays a critical role in maintaining an allocentric reference frame.
source: The results above demonstrate the action of the path-integration mechanism. It tracks the observer's location with respect to the external world during locomotion and plays a critical role in maintaining an allocentric reference frame.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: In the walking condition, the path-integration mechanism computes the traveled distance relative to the home base.
source: In the walking condition, the path-integration mechanism computes the traveled distance relative to the home base.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how the path-integration mechanism functions based on the experimental design and results.

claim: There was a small, though significant, difference between the divided attention walking condition and the baseline-stationary conditions (p = 0.022).
source: The average results in Figure 3d reveal a small, though significant, difference between the divided attention walking condition and the baseline-stationary conditions (p = 0.022).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis from Experiment 2.

claim: The distance underestimation in the divided attention walking condition was much smaller than that found in Experiment 1.
source: Noticeably, the distance underestimation in the divided attention walking condition (Figure 3d) was much smaller than that found in Experiment 1 (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental results from Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Path integration is less effective when observers are engaged in another mental task that distracts their spatial attention.
source: This suggests path integration is less effective when observers were engaged in another mental task that distracted their spatial attention.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results from Experiment 2.

claim: Judged target locations in the vestibular-forward condition were similar to the walking condition (p = 0.718).
source: Figure 4a reveals the judged target locations in the vestibular-forward condition (blue squares) were similar to the walking condition (green triangles; p = 0.718), and were significantly nearer than the baseline-stationary condition (red circles; p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis from Experiment 3.

claim: Judged target locations in the vestibular-forward condition were significantly nearer than the baseline-stationary condition (p < 0.0001).
source: Figure 4a reveals the judged target locations in the vestibular-forward condition (blue squares) were similar to the walking condition (green triangles; p = 0.718), and were significantly nearer than the baseline-stationary condition (red circles; p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis from Experiment 3.

claim: The path-integration mechanism can function during passive movements that stimulate the vestibular system.
source: This indicates the path-integration mechanism can function during passive movements that stimulate the vestibular system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the vestibular-forward condition results in Experiment 3.

claim: Backward displacement caused judged target locations to be farther than the baseline-stationary condition (p < 0.0001).
source: As expected, the backward displacement caused judged target locations to be farther than the baseline-stationary condition (p < 0.0001; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis from Experiment 3.

claim: The path-integration mechanism can sufficiently utilize the vestibular cue in both forward and backward moving directions.
source: Taken together, the experiment reveals the path-integration mechanism can sufficiently utilize the vestibular cue in both forward and backward moving directions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the vestibular-forward and vestibular-backward conditions in Experiment 3.

claim: Verbally reported distances were significantly shorter in the vestibular-forward than the baseline-stationary condition (p < 0.0001).
source: We found that verbally reported distances were significantly shorter in the vestibular-forward than the baseline-stationary condition (p < 0.0001, Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis from Experiment 4.

claim: Both the verbal report and blind walking-gesturing tasks show that forward moving in the dark before seeing the dimly lit target can affect judged target distance.
source: Thus, both the verbal report (Figure 4e) and blind walking-gesturing (Figure 4a) tasks show that forward moving in the dark before seeing the dimly lit target can affect judged target distance.
evidence: This is a comparison of results from different response tasks, showing consistency across methods.

claim: When the observer travels on a sloping surface in the dark, the visual system would not be able to simultaneously maintain the intrinsic bias at the home base in the vertical and horizontal directions.
source: This dependence on the ground surface, that is, an ecological constraint, predicts when the observer travels on a sloping surface in the dark, the visual system would not be able to simultaneously maintain the intrinsic bias at the home base in the vertical and horizontal directions.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the ecological constraint hypothesis, tested in Experiment 5.

claim: The intrinsic bias would be spatially updated in the horizontal but not in the vertical direction when descending a stepladder.
source: As the self-motion here consisted of both horizontal forward and vertical downward vectors, we predicted the intrinsic bias would be spatially updated in the horizontal but not in the vertical direction.
evidence: This is a prediction tested in Experiment 5.

claim: The judged horizontal distances were significantly shorter in the horizontal-walking condition than in the baseline-stationary condition (p < 0.001).
source: A comparison between the horizontal-walking and the baseline-stationary conditions reveals the judged horizontal distances were significantly shorter in the horizontal-walking condition (p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis from Experiment 5.

claim: The two sets of data from horizontal-walking and baseline-stationary conditions are fitted by the same intrinsic bias profile with a horizontal separation of 1.0 m.
source: The two sets of data are fitted by the same intrinsic bias profile with a horizontal separation of 1.0 m, which is close to the walked distance (1.06 m) in the horizontal-walking condition.
evidence: This is an analysis of the experimental data from Experiment 5.

claim: The horizontal separation of 1.0 m is close to the walked distance (1.06 m) in the horizontal-walking condition.
source: The two sets of data are fitted by the same intrinsic bias profile with a horizontal separation of 1.0 m, which is close to the walked distance (1.06 m) in the horizontal-walking condition.
evidence: This is a comparison of the fitted parameter to the experimental condition.

claim: The judged horizontal distances in the stepladder condition were significantly shorter than that in the baseline-stationary condition (p < 0.001).
source: The judged horizontal distances in the stepladder condition were significantly shorter than that in the baseline-stationary condition (p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis from Experiment 5.

claim: While descending the stepladder, the visual system spatially updated the horizontal but not the vertical vector of the intrinsic bias.
source: This confirms the prediction that while descending the stepladder, the visual system spatially updated the horizontal but not the vertical vector of the intrinsic bias (blue intrinsic bias, Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stepladder condition results in Experiment 5.

claim: The data from the stepladder and the horizontal-walking conditions overlap substantially.
source: Further supporting this, we found the data from the stepladder and the horizontal-walking conditions overlap substantially.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: When stepping down from a stepladder, the horizontal coordinate of the intrinsic bias is kept at the home base on the floor while the vertical coordinate moves downward with the body.
source: Taken together, our experiment revealed when stepping down from a stepladder, the horizontal coordinate of the intrinsic bias is kept at the home base on the floor while the vertical coordinate moves downward with the body.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 5.

claim: Human's path-integration mechanism operates much more efficiently along the horizontal ground plane than in the vertical direction.
source: This suggests human's path-integration mechanism, responsible for allocentric spatial coding, operates much more efficiently along the horizontal ground plane than in the vertical direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the asymmetric results in Experiment 5.

claim: Previous studies on spatial memory revealed the path-integration systems of land-dwelling animals are more efficient in estimating horizontally traveled distance.
source: The current finding on the vertical–horizontal asymmetry of the path-integration mechanism for visual space perception is consistent with previous studies on spatial memory, which revealed the path-integration systems of land-dwelling animals are more efficient in estimating horizontally traveled distance (Wohlgemuth et al., 2001; Jovalekic et al., 2011; Hayman et al., 2011; Zwergal et al., 2016; Ronacher, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Desert ants used path integration to return from foraging excursions on a shortcut way to their nests.
source: Wohlgemuth et al., 2001 found desert ants used path integration to return from foraging excursions on a shortcut way to their nests (also see Ronacher, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: When desert ants were crawling over a slope surface with uphill and downhill trajectory, their path-integration system computed only the horizontal component of the traveled distance.
source: Specifically, it was revealed when the ants were crawling over a slope surface with uphill and downhill trajectory, their path-integration system computed only the horizontal component of the traveled distance.
evidence: This claim is based on cited research about desert ants.

claim: The visual system can create a world-centered visual space by anchoring its spatial reference frame to the ground during navigation.
source: Overall, our study suggests the visual system can create a world-centered visual space by anchoring its spatial reference frame to the ground during navigation.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings.

claim: When we travel, the spatial representations of most surrounding objects, which are static relative to the ground, will remain constant despite the retinal image motion.
source: One advantage of adopting this space coding strategy is that when we travel, the spatial representations of most surrounding objects, which are static relative to the ground, will remain constant (static) despite the retinal image motion.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional advantage of the allocentric coding strategy.

claim: The visual system only needs to dynamically update the spatial representations of our bodies and the few objects that are moving relative to an allocentric origin on the ground.
source: Accordingly, our visual system only needs to dynamically update the spatial representations of our bodies and the few objects that are moving relative to an allocentric origin on the ground (within a world-centered context).
evidence: This is an inference about the computational efficiency of the allocentric coding strategy.

claim: A consequential byproduct of operating within the framework of an allocentric, world-centered visual space is the perceived stability of our visual environment during locomotion.
source: A consequential byproduct of operating within the framework of an allocentric, world-centered visual space is the perceived stability of our visual environment during locomotion.
evidence: This is an inference about the perceptual consequence of the allocentric coding strategy.

claim: The separation between perceived target locations before and after walking is smaller with allocentric coding than with egocentric coding.
source: Noticeably, the perceived target locations differ before (open red circle) and after walking (closed circle) as shown in both figures. However, the separation between the perceived target locations is smaller in Figure 2d (allocentric coding) than Figure 2e (egocentric coding), indicating more perceived location stability in the former.
evidence: This is a comparison of predictions from the two hypotheses illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Allocentric coding provides more perceived location stability than egocentric coding.
source: However, the separation between the perceived target locations is smaller in Figure 2d (allocentric coding) than Figure 2e (egocentric coding), indicating more perceived location stability in the former.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of the two coding strategies.

claim: Perceived target locations after a short walk are more underestimated with allocentric coding than with egocentric coding.
source: Although, this position stability has an accuracy trade-off as the perceived target locations after the short walk are more underestimated in Figure 2d (allocentric) than Figure 2e (egocentric).
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The location inaccuracy from using the allocentric spatial coding strategy will be minimized in the full cue environment, where the influence of the intrinsic bias is less.
source: Nevertheless, there is reason to believe that the location inaccuracy from using the allocentric spatial coding strategy will be minimized in the full cue environment, where the influence of the intrinsic bias is less.
evidence: This is speculation about how the allocentric strategy would perform in richer visual environments.

claim: When the ground is not visible in the dark, the surface slant of the intrinsic bias is responsible for the distance underestimation of a target on the ground.
source: This is because when the ground is not visible in the dark, the surface slant of the intrinsic bias is responsible for the distance underestimation of a target on the ground (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an explanation based on the intrinsic bias model illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: When there is sparse texture information on the ground, the ground surface representation becomes less slanted than the intrinsic bias and the distance underestimation error is less.
source: When there is some sparse texture information on the ground (Figure 1d), the ground surface representation becomes less slanted than the intrinsic bias and the distance underestimation error is less.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the integration model illustrated in Figure 1d.

claim: A full cue condition with rich texture gradient information on the ground will render the ground surface representation largely veridical, resulting in accurate distance perception.
source: Therefore, a full cue condition with rich texture gradient information on the ground will render the ground surface representation largely veridical, resulting in accurate distance perception.
evidence: This is speculation about performance in rich visual environments, based on the integration model.

claim: During observer self-motion, the brain establishes an allocentric intrinsic bias by employing the path-integration mechanism.
source: The observations reported here support the proposal that during observer self-motion the brain establishes an allocentric intrinsic bias by employing the path-integration mechanism.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by all the experimental findings.

claim: By utilizing the allocentric intrinsic bias, the visual system is able to construct an allocentric ground reference frame.
source: By utilizing the allocentric intrinsic bias, the visual system is able to construct an allocentric ground reference frame.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The ground-based visual space can effectively program and guide navigation of terrestrial creatures on the ground surface.
source: Accordingly, the ground-based visual space can effectively program and guide navigation of terrestrial creatures on the ground surface.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of the allocentric ground-based coding.

claim: The two-dimensional cognitive map employed by land-dwelling animals is linked to the terrain where they travel.
source: In this respect, we are reminded that the two-dimensional cognitive map (long-term spatial memory) employed by land-dwelling animals is also linked to the terrain where they travel (Jovalekic et al., 2011; Hayman et al., 2011; Tolman, 1948; O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Moser et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The intrinsic bias could be a function of the mammalian hippocampal formation.
source: Therefore, it is reasonable to speculate that the intrinsic bias could be a function of the mammalian hippocampal formation that is well known to be responsible for directing navigation when spatial sensory inputs are impoverished or lacking such as in the dark.
evidence: This is speculation about the neural basis of the intrinsic bias.

claim: The mammalian hippocampal formation mediates a representation of visual space that is stably anchored to the external world.
source: Consistent with this speculation, Nau et al., 2018 pointed to growing evidence that 'the mammalian hippocampal formation, extensively studied in the context of navigation and memory, mediates a representation of visual space that is stably anchored to the external world' (Nau et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The intrinsic bias that represents the internal model of the visual ground surface is implemented in the spatial memory system.
source: Following this line of thinking, we further speculate that the intrinsic bias that represents the internal model of the visual ground surface is implemented in the spatial memory system.
evidence: This is speculation about the neural implementation of the intrinsic bias.

claim: The spatial memory systems of land dwellers employ the same spatial coding, with the cognitive map serving as an internal model of the ground and the associated spatial features.
source: It is thus tempting to adopt the idea that the spatial memory systems of land dwellers employ the same spatial coding, with the cognitive map serving as an internal model of the ground and the associated spatial features (walls and obstacles) that are supported by the ground.
evidence: This is speculation about the relationship between spatial memory and visual perception systems.

claim: The intrinsic bias is the basis not only for the cognitive map within the medial temporal lobe but also for visual ground surface representation within the perceptual cortex.
source: As such, the intrinsic bias is the basis not only for the cognitive map within the medial temporal lobe but also for visual ground surface representation within the perceptual cortex (Byrne et al., 2007; Bottini and Doeller, 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The concept of the intrinsic bias could be genetically or epigenetically coded.
source: Future investigations should explore the broader notion that the concept of the intrinsic bias could be genetically or epigenetically coded, serving as an important priori knowledge for the brain to represent the ground surface and to construct our inner spatial world (Gibson, 1950; Kant, 1963; Von Uexküll, 2013).
evidence: This is speculation about the origins of the intrinsic bias, supported by citations to theoretical works.

claim: The intrinsic bias serves as important priori knowledge for the brain to represent the ground surface and to construct our inner spatial world.
source: Future investigations should explore the broader notion that the concept of the intrinsic bias could be genetically or epigenetically coded, serving as an important priori knowledge for the brain to represent the ground surface and to construct our inner spatial world (Gibson, 1950; Kant, 1963; Von Uexküll, 2013).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of the intrinsic bias, supported by citations to theoretical works.

claim: When performing spatial memory tasks in conditions where visual cues are not visible in the dark, the path-integration mechanism computes the traveled distance based on idiothetic distance information from the vestibular, proprioceptive, and efference copy of motor control signals.
source: Previous studies have found that when performing spatial memory tasks, in conditions where visual cues are not visible in the dark, the path-integration mechanism computes the traveled distance based on (non-visual) idiothetic distance information, such as from the vestibular, proprioceptive, and efference copy of motor control signals (Mittelstaedt and Mittelstaedt, 1980; Etienne et al., 1996; Loomis et al., 1999; Loomis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Natural scenes are largely enveloped by the prevalent sky above us and the ground on which we stand.
source: (a) and (b) Natural scenes are largely enveloped by the prevalent sky above us and the ground on which we stand.
evidence: This is a general observation about natural scenes, illustrated in Figure 1a and 1b.

claim: Target locations are judged with respect to the ground surface, which is our terrestrial niche.
source: Evidence suggests target locations are judged with respect to the ground surface, which is our terrestrial niche.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the literature and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The visual system uses the intrinsic bias as an implicit semi-elliptical surface representation in the dark to locate a dimly lit target.
source: (c) The visual system uses the intrinsic bias, an implicit semi-elliptical surface representation in the dark (illustrated as dashed white curve), to locate a dimly lit target (illustrated as unfilled green disc).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1c and supported by cited research.

claim: The target is perceived at the intersection between the projection line from the eye to the target and the intrinsic bias.
source: The target is perceived (filled green disc) at the intersection between the projection line from the eye to the target and the intrinsic bias.
evidence: This is the mechanism of target localization illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: The intrinsic bias acts like the visual system's internal model of the ground surface.
source: Essentially, the intrinsic bias acts like the visual system's internal model of the ground surface.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the function of the intrinsic bias.

claim: When the ground becomes visible, the intrinsic bias integrates with the visible depth cues to form a ground surface representation.
source: (d) When the ground becomes visible, the intrinsic bias integrates with the visible depth cues to form a ground surface representation, which serves as a reference frame to code target location.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1d and supported by cited research.

claim: The parallel rows of texture elements on the ground provide the depth cue for the visual system to construct a ground surface representation that is less slanted than the intrinsic bias.
source: For example, the parallel rows of texture elements on the ground (illustrated as filled red circles) provide the depth cue for the visual system to construct a ground surface representation (solid white curve) that is less slanted than the intrinsic bias.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1d.

claim: A ground surface representation less slanted than the intrinsic bias leads to more accurate target localization than in the dark.
source: This leads to a more accurate target localization than in the dark (c).
evidence: This is a comparison between the conditions illustrated in Figure 1c and 1d.

claim: The allocentric hypothesis predicts the intrinsic bias remains at the home base when the observer walks forward to a new location.
source: (b) The allocentric hypothesis predicts when the observer walks forward from the home base (illustrated as blue cross) to a new location (illustrated as red cross), the visual system relies on the path-integration mechanism to keep the intrinsic bias (illustrated as dashed blue curve) at the home base while monitoring the homing error vector (illustrated as white arrow).
evidence: This is the prediction of the allocentric hypothesis illustrated in Figure 2b.

claim: The egocentric hypothesis predicts the intrinsic bias tags along with the observer's body when walking to a new location.
source: (c) The egocentric hypothesis predicts the intrinsic bias tags along with the observer's body (illustrated as gray intrinsic bias) when he/she walks to the new location (illustrated as red cross).
evidence: This is the prediction of the egocentric hypothesis illustrated in Figure 2c.

claim: According to the allocentric hypothesis, the observer would perceive the target to be nearer and higher after walking than if they had not walked from the home base.
source: According to the allocentric hypothesis, the intrinsic bias (blue) would remain at the home base. Thus, when he/she stops and is presented with a dimly lit test target (illustrated by the green ring), the observer would perceive the target to be nearer and higher (Figure 2b) than if he/she had not walked from the home base (Figure 2a; we shall dub this the baseline-stationary condition).
evidence: This is a prediction of the allocentric hypothesis illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: According to the egocentric hypothesis, the observer would perceive the target at the same location as in the baseline-stationary condition after walking.
source: In contrast, if the intrinsic bias had moved along with the observer to the new location (illustrated as the gray curve in Figure 2c), as predicted by the alternative egocentric hypothesis, the observer would perceive the target at the same location as that in the baseline-stationary condition (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a prediction of the egocentric hypothesis illustrated in Figure 2.
